findings.description: verify_credentials returns immediately (no bcrypt call) when the email is unknown, but performs a full bcrypt.verify when the email exists and only the password is wrong. This creates a measurable timing side-channel that could be used to distinguish 'unknown email' from 'wrong password' even though both paths return an identical 401 body/message (AC3 is met on message content, not on timing). Practical exploitability is low for this specific POC (only 2 demo accounts exist and their emails are already published in the committed .env.example), but the pattern would be a real user-enumeration vector if the account set grows beyond the 2 seeded demo personas.
findings.required_action: Optional hardening for a future story: perform a dummy hash.verify() against a fixed/precomputed hash on the unknown-email path so both branches take comparable time. Not required to block this PASS given the POC's fixed 2-account scope and the already-accepted MFA/lockout gaps (DEC-003), but should be tracked if the user set ever grows.

findings.description: The bcrypt==4.0.1 pin (added as a documented deviation to fix a real passlib==1.7.4/bcrypt>=4.1 incompatibility that was verified to 500 every login without the pin) is well-justified, disclosed, and does not introduce a materially different security posture from the already-approved passlib[bcrypt] dependency. bcrypt 4.0.1 is now a few minor versions behind current bcrypt releases.
findings.required_action: None required now. Recommend tracking an upgrade path (e.g. moving off passlib to bcrypt's native API, or waiting for a passlib release compatible with newer bcrypt) as a follow-up, not a blocker for this story.
